sections.overview: Ariteus flavescens is a fruit-eating leaf-nosed bat in the family Phyllostomidae. It is the only living species in its genus and is endemic to Jamaica.
sections.identification: Head-and-body length is about 50–60 mm in males and 63–67 mm in females; there is no visible tail. Males weigh about 9.2–12.9 g and females 12.4–13.1 g, and females also have a longer forearm. The fur is reddish brown above, paler below, with conspicuous white patches on the shoulders; the broad nose leaf has a distinctive V-shaped lower edge. It is related to Antillean tree bats in the tribe Stenodermatini, but its small size and unusual nose leaf distinguish it from those close relatives.
sections.habitat: It is native only to Jamaica, from sea level to about 1,500 m elevation. Records come from primary and secondary forest, pastures, river corridors, and cultivated fruit groves and plantations.
sections.diet: It eats fruit, including figs, naseberries (Manilkara zapota), and rose apples; field records also document feeding on fustic fruit. The precise diet is poorly studied, and insects may supplement the fruit.
sections.behavior: This is a nocturnal, tree-roosting bat that begins flying and feeding around dusk. Researchers have captured it in forest, pasture-edge trees, orchards, and cultivated fruit plantations, rather than treating caves as its regular roost.
sections.reproduction: The limited records suggest births may occur more than once in a year: pregnant females were recorded in April and June–July, and lactating females in June–July. The small sample does not establish the timing of breeding throughout the island.
sections.ecology: At dusk it can join mixed-species feeding gatherings at fruit trees; field workers observed it sharing fruit with other Jamaican bats. This places it among the nocturnal consumers of both native forest and cultivated crops.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment published in 2019 classified it as Least Concern, based on its broad habitat tolerance and presumed large population; the population trend remains unknown and severe hurricanes are a potential threat.
